svg.title: Without token-boundary preemption a long background turn holds a decode slot and inverts priority; with it, the foreground agent is admitted at the next step and the background turn resumes from its resident KV cache
svg.desc: A two-panel timeline diagram on a dark slate-indigo background. A shared horizontal time axis runs from 0 to 32 seconds. The top panel, labelled no preemption, shows one decode slot on an RX 9070 XT occupied by a long background coding turn, a 940-token refactor that runs about 24 seconds. A foreground turn arrives at 4 seconds, marked by a cyan dashed line, but cannot get a slot: a red hatched wait bar stretches from 4 to 24 seconds, twenty seconds of blocking, annotated as priority inversion because a low-priority long turn is holding the slot the high-priority foreground turn needs. The foreground turn only starts decoding at 24 seconds. The bottom panel, labelled token-boundary preemption, shows the same background turn, but at the 4-second arrival it is paused at the next token boundary, drawn as a faded dashed segment, and the foreground turn starts almost immediately, within about 26 milliseconds, runs its roughly 9-second turn, and the background turn then resumes from its KV cache which stayed resident in the 16 gigabytes of VRAM, so there is no swap to host memory and no recompute. A footnote gives the model: 8 decode slots, about 39 tokens per second each, a coding-turn mixture with a 354-token mean, foreground wait for a free slot has a p99 of 6.2 seconds without preemption versus about 29 milliseconds with it.
svg.text: A long background turn holds a decode slot until preemption lets the foreground in
One RX 9070 XT, Qwen3.5-9B: 8 decode slots at ~39 tok/s each. A coding-turn mixture with a 354-token mean means most turns are short,
but the tail runs long. When the foreground turn lands behind a long one, the slot is busy for the whole turn unless you preempt.
No preemption — foreground waits out the running turn
Token-boundary preemption — foreground admitted at the next step
background resumes from resident KV — no swap, no recompute
From a discrete-event model of 8 slots serving a 354-token coding mixture: foreground wait for a free slot is p50 0.8 s, p90 2.5 s, p99 6.2 s, worst ~31 s without preemption.
Token-boundary preemption caps the wait at one decode step (~29 ms at p99), independent of how long the background turn runs. KV stays resident in 16 GB VRAM.
